I found several recent research articles related to Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models with focus on robustness, training methodologies, and data quality in 2025-2026. Here are the key findings:

## Robustness and Noise Training

VLA models' robustness to real-world perturbations is critical for deployment, and researchers recently evaluated the robustness of mainstream VLAs under 17 perturbations across four modalities. Research found that actions are the most fragile modality, existing visual-robust VLAs do not gain robustness in other modalities, and π0 demonstrates superior robustness.

To build multi-modal robust VLAs, researchers proposed RobustVLA against perturbations in VLA inputs and outputs, performing offline robust optimization against worst-case action noise that maximizes mismatch in flow matching objective, which can be seen as adversarial training, label smoothing, and outlier penalization.

## Data Quality and Training

A demonstration dataset is a key component for training VLA models, and there is a pressing need for a larger and more diverse set of demonstration data to train generalist VLA models that can handle a wide range of tasks.

Data collection involves hand-designed motion policies with injected noise for diversity and robustness.

## RL-Based Training Approaches

VLA model training predominantly relies on supervised fine-tuning through behavioral cloning of demonstration labels, and this approach is inherently susceptible to compounding errors under distribution shift.

Recent work has explored using reinforcement learning to improve VLA generalization and robustness beyond traditional supervised approaches.

Based on the search results, I found comprehensive information about SimpleVLA-RL, including details about SFT quality, ablation studies, data quality, and downstream RL performance:

## SimpleVLA-RL: SFT Quality, Ablation, and Downstream RL Performance

**SFT Quality and Data Scarcity:**

SimpleVLA-RL was tested using "One-Trajectory SFT" where only one demonstration data per task was used, utilizing merely 10 demonstration data per task suite across LIBERO's four task suites. With only a single demonstration per task, RL boosts LIBERO-Long success rates from 17.3% to 91.7%, and the performance gap between One-Trajectory SFT+RL and Full-Trajectory SFT+RL is minimal at 2.2%, indicating that RL can compensate for limited demonstration data.

**Downstream RL Performance:**

On four LIBERO task suites, SimpleVLA-RL improves the average success rate of the SFT-tuned OpenVLA-OFT model from 91% to 99%, achieving SoTA performance. On the LIBERO suite, applying SimpleVLA-RL to OpenVLA-OFT lifts the SFT baseline success rate from ~91% to 99%, with long-horizon tasks improving by ~12 percentage points, and RL objectives led to 7.8–13.3% gains. For RoboTwin dual-arm tasks, average success rates climb from 39.8% to 70.4% (RoboTwin1.0) and by 22–30% points (RoboTwin2.0).

**Generalization and Data Quality Effects:**

Generalization analysis reveals that SFT suffers from overfitting and catastrophic forgetting on unseen tasks, while SimpleVLA-RL maintains or improves performance on out-of-distribution tasks across spatial, object, and goal dimensions. On spatial generalization tasks, traditional SFT models show severe performance degradation, with success rates dropping to 0% on some unseen configurations, while SimpleVLA-RL consistently improves performance across all unseen spatial arrangements, achieving gains of 28.5% on one task and 7.1% to 13.3% on others.

Based on the search results, here's information about the "When Do Curricula Work?" paper by Wu et al. at ICLR 2021:

## Key Findings

For standard benchmark datasets, curricula have only marginal benefits, and randomly ordered samples perform as well or better than curricula and anti-curricula, suggesting that any benefit is entirely due to the dynamic training set size.

## When Curricula Do Work

The researchers investigated the role of limited training time budget and noisy data in the success of curriculum learning, and found that curriculum learning, but not anti-curriculum or random ordering, can improve performance either with limited training time budget or in the existence of noisy data.

## Research Methodology

The researchers conducted extensive experiments over thousands of orderings spanning three kinds of learning: curriculum, anti-curriculum, and random-curriculum -- in which the size of the training dataset is dynamically increased over time.

This paper was accepted at ICLR 2021 for Oral Presentation.

The paper provides insights into when ordering training examples by difficulty actually helps, showing that the main benefits come from having a dynamically growing dataset rather than the specific ordering, except in specific practical scenarios like limited training budgets or noisy data.

Based on the search results, I found relevant information about D-SPEAR:

## D-SPEAR: Dual-Stream Prioritized Experience Adaptive Replay

D-SPEAR is a replay framework that decouples actor and critic sampling while maintaining a shared replay buffer. The critic leverages prioritized replay for efficient value learning, whereas the actor is updated using low-error transitions to stabilize policy optimization.

### Key Problem It Addresses

Robotic manipulation remains challenging for reinforcement learning due to contact-rich dynamics, long horizons, and training instability. Although off-policy actor-critic algorithms such as SAC and TD3 perform well in simulation, they often suffer from policy oscillations and performance collapse in realistic settings, partly due to experience replay strategies that ignore the differing data requirements of the actor and the critic.

### Core Technical Features

An adaptive anchor mechanism balances uniform and prioritized sampling based on the coefficient of variation of TD errors, and a Huber-based critic objective further improves robustness under heterogeneous reward scales.

### Performance Results

D-SPEAR was evaluated on challenging robotic manipulation tasks from the robosuite benchmark, including Block-Lifting and Door-Opening. Results demonstrate that D-SPEAR consistently outperforms strong off-policy baselines, including SAC, TD3, and DDPG, in both final performance and training stability, with ablation studies confirming the complementary roles of the actor-side and critic-side replay streams.

The paper was published on arXiv in March/April 2026 by Yu Zhang and Karl Mason.

I found comprehensive information about SCIZOR. Here's what the search revealed:

## Overview

SCIZOR is a self-supervised data curation framework that filters out low-quality state-action pairs to improve the performance of imitation learning policies. The paper was accepted to the 2026 IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation (ICRA).

## Key Problem

Large-scale datasets used for policy training often introduce substantial variability in quality, which can negatively impact performance, making automatically curating datasets by filtering low-quality samples essential. Existing robotic curation approaches rely on costly manual annotations and perform curation at a coarse granularity, such as the dataset or trajectory level, failing to account for the quality of individual state-action pairs.

## Approach

SCIZOR targets two complementary sources of low-quality data: suboptimal data, which hinder learning with undesirable actions, and redundant data, which dilute training with repetitive patterns.

The framework uses two main components:
- A progress-prediction model flags and removes frames that fail to make meaningful task progress, without needing reward signals
- Joint visual-action embeddings are clustered to detect and discard look-alike segments, ensuring diversity

## Results

SCIZOR improves policy performance across diverse large-scale imitation learning benchmarks, showing on average 15.4% improvement.

## Authors

The paper is authored by Yu Zhang, Yuqi Xie, Huihan Liu, Rutav Shah, Michael Wan, Linxi Fan, and Yuke Zhu.

Based on the search results, here's what I found about LIBERO-Plus:

## Overview

LIBERO-Plus is a comprehensive benchmark designed to establish a rigorous leaderboard for evaluating generalization capabilities across key vulnerability dimensions for Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models in robotic manipulation tasks.

## Perturbation Dimensions

The benchmark introduces controlled perturbations across seven dimensions: objects layout, camera viewpoints, robot initial states, language instructions, light conditions, background textures and sensor noise.

## Key Findings

The research revealed significant weaknesses in current VLA models:

- **Extreme Sensitivity**: Models exhibit extreme sensitivity to perturbation factors, including camera viewpoints and robot initial states, with performance dropping from 95% to below 30% under modest perturbations.

- **Language Ignorance**: Models are largely insensitive to language variations, with further experiments revealing that models tend to ignore language instructions completely.

- **Compositional Generalization Gap**: Models fail catastrophically when multiple perturbations occur simultaneously, and researchers introduced the concept of Compositional Generalization Gap to quantitatively measure model performance under combined perturbations.

## Benchmark Structure

The benchmark construction follows a systematic two-stage process: expanding the original LIBERO benchmark through seven distinct perturbation factors, followed by task filtering and category balancing, and then evaluating using representative models and stratifying tasks into five difficulty levels. LIBERO-Plus is an extensive benchmark with 10,030 tasks spanning seven perturbation dimensions.

I found comprehensive search results on this topic. Here's what I found:

## Main Finding: iw-SFT Paper

The primary work on importance weighted supervised fine-tuning (iw-SFT) is a method that modifies SFT to optimize a tighter bound to the RL objective. The research clarifies that SFT can be understood as maximizing a lower bound on the RL objective in a sparse reward setting.

## Key Contribution

A small modification to SFT leads to an importance weighted variant that behaves closer to training with RL as it: i) optimizes a tighter bound to the RL objective and, ii) can improve performance compared to SFT on curated data. The method is easy to implement and can be further generalized to training with quality scored data.

## Performance Results

The resulting SFT variants are competitive with more advanced RL algorithms for large language models and for training policies in continuous control tasks, for example achieving 66.7% on the AIME 2024 dataset.

## Related Concurrent Work

The search also revealed related concurrent work on this topic. Qin & Springenberg (2025) reframe SFT as a lower bound of RL and improve it by introducing importance weighting based on the data-generating policy. Additionally, DFT (Dynamic Fine-Tuning) outperforms the concurrent Importance-Weighted SFT (iw-SFT) in most settings across model families and benchmarks, achieving higher average accuracy on most model families.

**Demonstration-based Robot Learning:**
Pretraining deep reinforcement learning (DRL) with prior expert demonstrations, along with continuous training with online data, has shown impressive performance in exploration efficiency. **Adaptive Sampling Approaches:**
Adaptive sampling methods like the Rapidly-Exploring Adaptive Sampling Tree* (RAST*) and Gaussian Mixture Regression RRT* leverage an adaptive sampling approach to prioritize information-dense regions, effectively reducing localization uncertainty by concentrating on areas with higher information gain.

**Multi-Skill Learning with Adaptive Selection:**
An adaptive command sampling mechanism balances training across skills of varying difficulty and prevents catastrophic forgetting. The Seamless Multi-Skill Learning (SMSL) framework leverages high-quality historical experiences to guide skill acquisition with an adaptive command sampling mechanism.

**Sample Prioritization:**
Recent work decomposes reward values into independent components and proposes reward learning algorithms by prioritizing data samples based on their prompt-free reward values.

These approaches represent current advances in making robot learning more efficient through intelligent sampling and prioritization of training data.

Based on the search results, here's what I found about these two related but distinct approaches:

## Rho-1 (NeurIPS 2024)

Rho-1 is a language model that employs Selective Language Modeling (SLM), which selectively trains on useful tokens that aligned with the desired distribution. This approach involves scoring training tokens using a reference model, and then training the language model with a focused loss on tokens with higher scores.

When continual pretraining on 15B OpenWebMath corpus, Rho-1 yields an absolute improvement in few-shot accuracy of up to 30% in 9 math tasks. After fine-tuning, Rho-1-1B and 7B achieved state-of-the-art results of 40.6% and 51.8% on MATH dataset, respectively – matching DeepSeekMath with only 3% of the pretraining tokens.

## RHO-LOSS (ICML 2022)

Reducible Holdout Loss Selection (RHO-LOSS) is a simple but principled technique which selects approximately those points for training that most reduce the model's generalization loss. RHO-LOSS selects points that are learnable, worth learning, and not yet learnt.

On the large web-scraped image dataset Clothing-1M, RHO-LOSS trains in 18x fewer steps and reaches 2% higher final accuracy than uniform data shuffling.

The key connection is that both methods use a reference model to guide data selection, though Rho-1 operates at the token level for language models while RHO-LOSS operates at the point/sample level across various domains.

## Paper Found: "Why Does Self-Distillation (Sometimes) Degrade the Reasoning Capability of LLMs?"

Self-distillation has emerged as an effective post-training paradigm for LLMs, often improving performance while shortening reasoning traces. However, in mathematical reasoning, it can reduce response length while degrading performance.

### Main Finding: Epistemic Suppression

The degradation is traced to the suppression of epistemic verbalization - the model's expression of uncertainty during reasoning. Conditioning the teacher on rich information suppresses uncertainty expression, enabling rapid in-domain optimization with limited task coverage but harming OOD performance, where unseen problems benefit from expressing uncertainty and adjusting accordingly.

### EMA Feedback Loop

Your query specifically mentioned the EMA (exponential moving average) feedback loop. SDPO uses an EMA-smoothed teacher (EMA rate: 0.05). However, setting the EMA rate to 0.0 (i.e., fixing the teacher to the initial policy) yields better performance. Additionally, a moving target teacher, even with slow EMA updates, amplifies epistemic suppression through a feedback loop, where the student learns from an increasingly confident teacher, leading to greater performance degradation.

### Performance Impact

Across Qwen3-8B, DeepSeek-Distill-Qwen-7B, and Olmo3-7B-Instruct, performance drops of up to 40% are observed.

The paper (arXiv 2603.24472) was published on March 25, 2026, by researchers from Microsoft Research, KAIST, and Seoul National University.

# Key Technical Components of iw-SFT

## (1) Main Theorem: SFT as RL Lower Bound

The paper establishes that standard SFT on filtered data optimizes a lower bound on the RL objective. Using the inequality x ≥ 1 + log(x), they derive:

**"J(θ) ≥ 𝔼_πref(τ)[R(τ) log p(τ;θ)] + const"**

This bound becomes looser as training progresses and the learned policy diverges from the reference distribution.

## (2) Auxiliary Distribution q(τ): Time-Lagged Policy

The auxiliary distribution is formulated as a parametric policy with lagged parameters:

**"q(τ) = p(s₀) ∏ₜ p(sₜ₊₁|sₜ,aₜ) π(aₜ|sₜ;θ_q)"**

where θ_q gradually approaches θ during training. This allows q to track the evolving policy while remaining stable.

## (3) EMA Implementation

Yes, the paper explicitly mentions exponential moving average for continuous control. For D4RL experiments, they implement: **"θ_q = α·θ_q + (1-α)·θ"** updated during each optimization step, similar to target networks in deep RL algorithms.

## (4) Importance-Weighted SFT Objective

The core contribution yields:

**"𝒥_iw-SFT = 𝔼_τ∈𝒟⁺[q(τ)/πref(τ) log p(τ;θ)]"**

This tightens the bound by reweighting samples, allowing "adaptive filtering" that emphasizes preferred trajectories.

## (5) Continuous Control & Robotics

The paper demonstrates generality across domains: D4RL locomotion tasks (halfcheetah, hopper, walker2d), maze navigation, and Franka kitchen manipulation. Results show iw-SFT(Q) competitive with offline RL baselines like CQL and IQL.

# Analysis of iw-SFT Paper: Auxiliary Distribution q(τ) Implementation Details

## (1) EMA Usage: LLM vs. Continuous Control

The paper uses **different update mechanisms** for q across domains:

- **LLM setting**: Uses time-lagged parameters without explicit EMA. The text states: "we set θq to be a time-lagged version of θ, the parameters we are optimizing" with details deferred to experiments.

- **Continuous Control**: Explicitly employs exponential moving average: "instead of updating...q at discrete time-points we use exponential weight averaging θq=αθq+(1−α)θ during each step."

The EMA approach is **specific to D4RL**, not generalized across settings.

## (2) Loss Function Used by q

The paper uses **importance weights only**, not reducible/excess loss. The auxiliary distribution q computes trajectory probabilities directly via standard policy likelihood: "q(τ)=p(s₀)∏t p(st+1|st,at)π(at|st;θq)". These become importance weight ratios q(τ)/πref(τ) in the objective.

## (3) EMA Generality

The exponential moving average "is similar to how target networks in continuous control RL algorithms are often updated." This positioning suggests the mechanism is **domain-specific engineering** rather than a proposed general principle applicable across settings.

## (4) Prioritized Experience Replay Discussion

**No discussion of PER-style prioritized sampling** appears in the paper. The approach weights trajectories multiplicatively in the loss rather than using them for sample selection probability.

## (5) Application to Imitation Learning, Robotics, or VLAs

The paper **does not discuss these domains**. Experiments focus exclusively on mathematical reasoning (LLMs) and D4RL locomotion tasks. The Franka Kitchen experiment (Section 4.3) involves robotic simulation but receives minimal treatment and doesn't explore broader robotics or vision-language applications.

## Overview

The paper titled "Dynamic Loss-Based Sample Reweighting for Improved Large Language Model Pretraining" was submitted to ICLR 2025.

## Key Contributions

The paper introduces novel algorithms for dynamic, instance-level data reweighting aimed at improving both the efficiency and effectiveness of LLM pretraining. The methods adjust the weight of each training sample based on its loss value in an online fashion, allowing the model to dynamically focus on more informative or important samples at the current training stage.

The framework systematically devises reweighting strategies deprioritizing redundant or uninformative data.

## Theoretical and Empirical Results

The authors develop a new theoretical framework for analyzing the impact of loss-based reweighting on the convergence of gradient-based optimization, providing the first formal characterization of how these strategies affect convergence bounds.

Empirical validation spans a spectrum of tasks, from pretraining 7B and 1.4B parameter LLMs to smaller-scale language models and linear regression problems, demonstrating that the loss-based reweighting approach can lead to faster convergence and significantly improved performance.

## Reweighting Strategies

The research introduces novel dynamic instance-level loss-based reweighting strategies, such as LinUpper, Quadratic, and Extremes.

## Code Availability

The full code for large-scale LLM pretraining is available in IBM's FSDP foundation model stack, and there's also a public repository containing code for the ICLR 2025 paper.

## Overview

The paper titled "Dynamic Loss-Based Sample Reweighting for Improved Large Language Model Pretraining" was submitted to ICLR 2025.

## Key Contributions

The paper introduces novel algorithms for dynamic, instance-level data reweighting aimed at improving both the efficiency and effectiveness of LLM pretraining. The methods adjust the weight of each training sample based on its loss value in an online fashion, allowing the model to dynamically focus on more informative or important samples at the current training stage.

The framework systematically devises reweighting strategies deprioritizing redundant or uninformative data.

## Theoretical and Empirical Results

The authors develop a new theoretical framework for analyzing the impact of loss-based reweighting on the convergence of gradient-based optimization, providing the first formal characterization of how these strategies affect convergence bounds.

Empirical validation spans a spectrum of tasks, from pretraining 7B and 1.4B parameter LLMs to smaller-scale language models and linear regression problems, demonstrating that the loss-based reweighting approach can lead to faster convergence and significantly improved performance.

## Reweighting Strategies

The research introduces novel dynamic instance-level loss-based reweighting strategies, such as LinUpper, Quadratic, and Extremes.

The full code for large-scale LLM pretraining is available in IBM's FSDP foundation model stack, and there's also a public repository containing code for the ICLR 2025 paper.

## LEAD: Iterative Data Selection for Efficient LLM Instruction Tuning

LEAD is a paper on iterative data selection for efficient LLM instruction tuning, published in May 2025.

### Core Innovation: Instance-Level Dynamic Uncertainty (IDU)

LEAD introduces Instance-Level Dynamic Uncertainty (IDU), a theoretically grounded utility function combining instantaneous training loss, gradient-based approximation of loss changes, and exponential smoothing of historical loss signals.

### Key Advantages

IDU is computed entirely using training-time signals naturally available during model updates (losses and logits), thus incurring no additional inference overhead.

### Two-Stage Selection Strategy

LEAD employs a two-stage, coarse-to-fine selection strategy, adaptively prioritizing informative clusters through a multi-armed bandit mechanism, followed by precise fine-grained selection of high-utility samples using IDU.

### Experimental Results

Extensive experiments across four diverse benchmarks show that LEAD significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods, improving average model performance by 6.1%-10.8% while using only 2.5% of the training data and reducing overall training time by 5-10x.

### Problem Being Solved

Existing iterative model-aware data selection methods incur significant computational overhead, as they rely on repeatedly performing full-dataset model inference to estimate sample utility for subsequent training iterations. LEAD proposes an efficient iterative data selection framework that accurately estimates sample utility entirely within the standard training loop, eliminating the need for costly additional model inference.

Based on the search results, I found comprehensive information about "Freshness-Aware Prioritized Experience Replay for LLM/VLM Reinforcement Learning":

## Overview

Freshness-Aware PER is the first work to successfully apply PER to LLM/VLM reinforcement learning. The work addresses reinforcement learning in post-training Large Language Models (LLMs) and Vision-Language Models (VLMs), where on-policy algorithms such as PPO, GRPO, and REINFORCE++ are the dominant paradigm.

## The Problem It Solves

While Experience Replay drives sample efficiency in classic RL by allowing agents to reuse past trajectories and prioritize informative ones, directly applying Prioritized Experience Replay (PER) to LLMs fails because the rapid policy evolution of billion-parameter models renders stored priorities stale, causing old high-priority trajectories to dominate sampling long after they have become uninformative.

## The Solution

Freshness-Aware PER addresses the priority staleness problem by augmenting any PER-based priority with a multiplicative exponential age decay grounded in effective sample size analysis.

## Performance Results

The method was evaluated on eight multi-step agentic, reasoning, and math competition tasks with 0.5B, 3B, and 7B models, achieving +46% on NQ Search, +367% on Sokoban, and +133% on VLM FrozenLake, while standard PER without age decay consistently degrades performance.

The paper appears to be recent (April 2026) and addresses a critical challenge in improving sample efficiency for LLM/VLM training in reinforcement learning.

## Key Research Insights

**SFT as RL Initialization:**

SFT can provide a safe starting point and policy initialization, where the model can at least align the format and generate reasonable candidates for the reward model to evaluate. However, RL can hardly converge without SFT because the base model has poor task-following ability, which would give overwhelmingly low scores for RL, leading to unstable updates and collapse in training.

**Convergence Speed and Sample Efficiency:**

A recent approach called Dynamic Fine-Tuning (DFT) shows improvements over standard SFT. DFT demonstrates three distinct advantages: (1) Faster convergence, achieving peak performance within the first 120 training steps on most benchmarks; (2) Better early-stage performance, with DFT already outperforming best final accuracy of SFT within the first 10–20 steps; and (3) Higher sample efficiency, consistently requiring fewer updates to reach relatively optimal results.

**Robot Learning Applications:**

In an empirical study of Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models, RL fine-tuning versus SFT shows that RL enhances VLA generalization substantially in Execution, improves moderately in Semantics, and performs on par with SFT for Vision. Additionally, SFT saturates at 16k demonstrations, and at convergence, RL performs comparably to SFT-16k in the training setting and 42.6% better on unseen scenarios.

**Recent Findings (2025-2026):**

There is ongoing debate about the optimal SFT→RL pipeline. Despite RL's superior generalization, SFT remains essential for effective RL training; SFT stabilizes the model's output format, enabling subsequent RL to achieve its performance gains.

## Re-Mix: Optimizing Data Mixtures for Large Scale Imitation Learning

The paper is authored by Joey Hejna from Stanford University, along with Chethan Bhateja, Yichen Jiang, Karl Pertsch, and Dorsa Sadigh.

### Main Contribution

The work investigates how to weigh different subsets or "domains" of robotics datasets for robot foundation model pre-training, using distributionally robust optimization (DRO) to maximize worst-case performance across all possible downstream domains.

### Key Challenges and Solutions

The method, Re-Mix, addresses the wide range of challenges that arise when applying DRO to robotics datasets including variability in action spaces and dynamics across different datasets. More specifically, ReMix employs early stopping and action normalization and discretization to counteract these issues.

### Evaluation

Through extensive experimentation on both the Bridge and OpenX datasets, the authors demonstrate that data curation can have an outsized impact on downstream performance.

### Publication

The paper was published at the 8th Conference on Robot Learning (CoRL) in 2025, though it was initially released on arXiv in August 2024.

Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) is a critical step for adapting Large Language Models to specialized domains, often serving as an initialization for subsequent reinforcement learning. However, SFT can overfit a small set of expert data, harming generalization and eroding prior knowledge, which can limit downstream RL that benefits from a strong, generalizable initialization for exploration.

The research demonstrates that prior knowledge degradation primarily results from tokens in the expert data to which the base model assigns low probability. These low-probability tokens represent a significant deviation from the model's current prior knowledge. Due to the nature of the log-likelihood objective, they produce larger gradient magnitudes, which speed up adaptation to the new data but degrade generalization.

The paper studies the token-wise clipping strategy, a commonly used trust-region method for bounding per-token updates. It finds that clipping reshapes token-level learning priorities, promoting more progressive adaptation that fits the new data while preserving general abilities.

**Key Results:** Compared with standard SFT, clipping low-probability tokens reduces out-of-distribution forgetting by 11.54% and improves final RL performance by 7.09% across the agentic benchmarks. Moreover, latent-space analysis shows smaller representational drift under clipping, indicating that it provides a generalizable initialization.

This paper was presented as a poster at ICML 2026.

# Paper Analysis: Off-Policy Token Clipped SFT

## (1) Specific Problem with SFT Quality Affecting RL
The paper identifies that standard SFT suffers from "memorizing a small set of expert data" which causes "catastrophic forgetting of prior knowledge, undermining the promise of effective RL." The root issue stems from tokens where the base model has low probability assignments.

## (2) Robotics or VLA Models?
No. The work does not focus on robotics or vision-language models. It addresses general language model fine-tuning.

## (3) Benchmarks Used
The paper evaluates on two agentic benchmarks: **ALFWorld** and **ScienceWorld**.

## (4) Key Mechanism: Token-Level Clipping
The authors apply a clipping strategy to constrain "per-token updates within a trust region." This moderates learning by limiting gradient magnitudes from tokens with low model probabilities, creating "a more on-policy-like training dynamic."

## (5) Token-Level vs. Data-Level Filtering
Yes, this operates at the token level, not data level. The approach selectively constrains gradient updates for specific low-probability tokens rather than filtering entire training examples, allowing preservation of useful data while tempering destabilizing gradients.

## (6) SFT Data Quality Affecting RL Convergence
The paper does not explicitly discuss convergence speed. Instead, it reports that clipping "reduces forgetting on out-of-distribution tasks by 11.54% and boosts final RL performance by 7.09%."

## Curriculum Learning Benefits

Recent work shifts the focus of curriculum learning in multi-robot systems from scalability to improving long-term coordination, proposing strategies that gradually increase the length of expert trajectories during training to stabilize learning and enhance accuracy. Results show that curriculum learning improves long-term accuracy while perceptual estimation methods yield policies robust to realistic uncertainty.

## Data Prioritization Approaches

Recent frameworks like Active Skill-level Data Aggregation (ASkDAgger) enable human teachers to provide validation, relabeling, and annotation feedback, with a Prioritized Interactive Experience Replay (PIER) module that prioritizes using these mixed evaluative-and-corrective demonstrations during training to allow robots to learn both what not to do and what to do more efficiently.

## Handling Noisy Demonstrations

Methods have been developed to approximate egocentric robot perception from global state demonstrations by filtering neighbors, converting reference frames, and simulating onboard sensor variability. Demonstrations inherently contain inconsistencies, hesitations, and corrections that, when combined with natural sensor noise and calibration misalignments, can confuse learning algorithms and create unsafe robotic behaviors.

## General Imitation Learning Benefits

Reinforcement learning from demonstrations leverages both expert data and reward feedback to improve sample efficiency, guide exploration, and stabilise policy learning in high-dimensional robotic domains.

I've found several recent arXiv papers on Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models with relevant research on data curation and adaptive/online training from 2026:

## Key Recent Papers (2026)

**Green-VLA** - Dataset curation plus RL alignment builds on unified pretraining to progressively improve performance, with Green-VLA achieving the largest gains after RL alignment, especially on long-horizon success, recovery, and precise task following. The DataQA pipeline was employed for robotic dataset curation and quality assessment, enabling model training on high-quality demonstrations to improve both sample efficiency and final policy performance. The pipeline supports iterative model updates via RL fine-tuning and feedback from real-robot deployments.

**LingBot-VLA** - By scaling pre-training data from 3,000 hours to 20,000 hours, success rates improve consistently and substantially, showing no signs of saturation even at 20,000 hours, providing the first empirical evidence of favorable scaling properties in real-world robot learning for large-scale data curation.

**LoRA-SP (Adaptive Capacity Allocation)** - LoRA-SP is a rank-adaptive fine-tuning method that replaces fixed-rank updates with input- and layer-wise capacity, using an SVD-style parameterization with a small router whose nonnegative scores act as singular values over a shared vector bank.

**ACoT-VLA** - Action Chain-of-Thought forms a reasoning paradigm where the deliberative process is formulated as structured action intents, enabling grounded and long-horizon policy learning.

Additionally, The advancement of VLAs is intrinsically linked to the availability of large-scale, diverse, and well-structured training data and evaluation benchmarks, with the field seeing the curation of substantial datasets categorized into real-world and simulation-sourced collections.

content.text:
I've completed my independent research. Here is my review:

```json
{
  "verdict": "revise",
  "scores": {
    "novelty": {"score": 3, "rationale": "The combination of EMA reference + reducible loss + PER for VLA SFT is novel, but each component exists in prior work. Critically, iw-SFT (arXiv Jul 2025) already implements EMA (θ_q = α·θ_q + (1-α)·θ) for continuous control, narrowing the claimed novelty of Contribution 1. The SFT→RL pipeline finding is partially pre-empted by 'Clipping Low-Probability Tokens in SFT Yields a Generalizable Initialization for RL' (ICML 2026). The specific combination remains unpublished but the novelty ceiling is incremental."},
    "feasibility": {"score": 4, "rationale": "All dependencies (OpenVLA-OFT, SimpleVLA-RL, LIBERO) are open-source and accessible. Implementation is straightforward (EMA copy + reducible loss + proportional sampling). The CoRL 14-day sprint is very tight (13 days to abstract deadline today) but the minimum viable plan of 15 SFT + 4 RL runs on 8×A100 is achievable. AAAI 2027 timeline is comfortable."},
    "clarity": {"score": 4, "rationale": "Exceptionally well-written proposal with comprehensive landscape analysis covering 35+ references, honest novelty positioning, thorough experimental plan with calibrated expectations ('does no harm' on clean data), and transparent acknowledgment of limitations (EMA feedback risk, memorization capacity). The theoretical framework is well-motivated within iw-SFT."},
    "impact": {"score": 3, "rationale": "The RAPID+RL pipeline finding is the strongest impact argument, but 'What Can RL Bring to VLA Generalization?' shows SFT primarily affects convergence speed not ceiling, limiting practical impact. Primary gains are on noisy data (per 'When Do Curricula Work?'), a realistic but narrow setting. The ICML 2026 clipping paper establishes the same SFT→RL principle in a different domain, reducing the novelty premium of Contribution 4."}
  },
  "issues": [
    "MISSING REFERENCE: 'Clipping Low-Probability Tokens in SFT Yields a Generalizable Initialization for RL' (ICML 2026, poster). This paper directly studies how SFT technique quality affects downstream RL performance — showing 7.09% RL improvement and 11.54% reduced forgetting via token-level clipping. While it operates on LLMs (ALFWorld, ScienceWorld) at the token level rather than VLA data level, it establishes the same principle as RAPID's Contribution 4 ('SFT quality cascades to RL'). Must be cited. RAPID's differentiation: (a) data/demonstration-level filtering vs. token-level clipping, (b) VLA domain with action-prediction loss vs. LLM domain with language loss, (c) noise filtering mechanism vs. trust-region mechanism. This weakens the claim of 'first to study SFT quality → RL' — reframe as 'first to study SFT *data quality* → RL for *VLAs*.'",
    "NOVELTY NARROWING: iw-SFT (arXiv 2507.12856) already implements EMA update θ_q = α·θ_q + (1-α)·θ for continuous control (D4RL) experiments. The proposal's Contribution 1 claims 'RAPID introduces a purpose-built EMA reference specifically designed for data quality scoring' as if no EMA reference exists in supervised/IL settings — but iw-SFT uses exactly this mechanism for updating the auxiliary distribution q in continuous control SFT/BC. The critical distinction: iw-SFT uses EMA for trajectory-level importance weights (multiplicative loss reweighting), while RAPID uses EMA for *reducible loss computation* + *PER-style sampling priorities*. This distinction is real but must be articulated precisely. Reframe: 'iw-SFT proposed EMA for importance weighting; we use EMA for reducible loss decomposition, revealing that the EMA reference enables noise-robust prioritization beyond what importance weighting alone provides.'",
    "CoRL TIMELINE: 13 days to abstract deadline (May 26), 16 days to paper deadline (May 29). The proposal should include an explicit go/no-go decision point: if the first noise-injection experiment results are not available by ~May 22-23, fall back to AAAI 2027 only. The abstract deadline requires at least preliminary results to write a credible abstract.",
    "FINITE-T TESTABILITY: Corollary 1.1 predicts T₀ = C₁/(C₂·Δ₀·ε) falls within 'thousands of steps' for τ* = 0.978. However, the constants C₁, C₂ depend on loss landscape properties (Lipschitz constant M, gradient bound ε) that are difficult to estimate a priori for VLA models. The empirical crossover point may differ by an order of magnitude from the theoretical prediction. The proposal should acknowledge this uncertainty and frame the empirical bound-gap measurement as a test of the theory's qualitative prediction (linear vs quadratic growth) rather than its quantitative prediction (exact T₀).",
    "NOISE INJECTION VS REAL-WORLD NOISE: The primary experiment uses synthetic corruption (Gaussian noise, frame dropping, truncation). Real-world demonstration noise (hesitation, redundant motions, suboptimal strategies, operator fatigue) has fundamentally different structure — it's *coherent* noise that may be harder for reducible loss to detect. The OXE experiment (deferred to AAAI) would address this. For CoRL, acknowledge this limitation explicitly and frame noise injection as a controlled test of the mechanism, not a claim about real-world robustness."
  ],
  "feedback": "The proposal has reached an exceptionally high level of polish and the landscape analysis is now world-class. The remaining gap to 'pass' (avg 3.5 vs 4.0 threshold) reflects inherent novelty and impact ceilings rather than fixable oversights. Here is how to close the gap:\n\n**1. Cite and differentiate from ICML 2026 clipping paper (easy, high priority).** 'Clipping Low-Probability Tokens in SFT Yields a Generalizable Initialization for RL' establishes that SFT technique → RL performance in LLMs. RAPID's differentiation is clear: (a) data-level noise filtering vs. token-level trust region, (b) VLA domain vs. LLM domain, (c) prioritized sampling vs. gradient clipping. Frame RAPID as: 'The ICML 2026 work shows SFT technique affects RL for LLMs; we show SFT *data quality* affects RL for VLAs — a complementary finding in a different domain with a different mechanism.'\n\n**2. Sharpen iw-SFT differentiation (important).** iw-SFT already uses EMA for continuous control. RAPID's actual novelty over iw-SFT is threefold: (a) reducible loss decomposition (iw-SFT uses trajectory probabilities for importance weights, RAPID uses loss difference for noise-robust prioritization), (b) PER-style sampling (iw-SFT reweights loss multiplicatively, RAPID controls which samples are seen), (c) theoretical analysis of optimal τ and finite-T crossover. State this explicitly rather than claiming EMA reference as wholly novel.\n\n**3. The path to pushing impact from 3→4.** The single most impactful result would be a compelling RAPID+RL experiment showing e.g. 30-50% fewer RL steps to reach 90% success. If this materializes, lead the paper with it. The narrative becomes: 'SFT data quality is the hidden bottleneck of VLA RL pipelines; RAPID provides a drop-in fix.' This is more impactful than 'another data curation method for noisy demonstrations.'\n\n**4. Consider whether CoRL is the right target.** With 13 days to abstract, the risk of a rushed submission is high. The AAAI 2027 timeline (3+ months) allows comprehensive experiments including LIBERO-Plus and OXE, which would strengthen impact significantly. A well-executed AAAI paper with the RAPID+RL finding as headline result + robustness on LIBERO-Plus + OXE mixed-quality is stronger than a rushed CoRL submission. If you attempt CoRL, treat it as a stretch with explicit go/no-go by May 22.\n\n**5. For the next revision, focus on sharpening rather than expanding.** The proposal is comprehensive but very long. The landscape analysis is thorough but could be tightened. Every additional reference and caveat adds length but diminishing returns on clarity. The core story is: 'EMA-based reducible loss enables noise-robust, adaptive data prioritization for VLA SFT, and this cascades to faster RL convergence.' Everything should serve this narrative.",
  "reason": "Novelty and impact remain at 3/5 (avg 3.5 < 4.0): iw-SFT's existing EMA for continuous control and ICML 2026's SFT→RL finding further narrow the claimed contributions; the core combination is real but incremental."
}
```
